label: Translated Of Grammatology and extended deconstruction into postcolonial critique
description: Spivak's landmark English translation and critical preface to Derrida's Of Grammatology (1976) introduced deconstruction to the Anglophone world before redirecting Derridean aporia toward the colonial "native informant."
dialecticalTension: Politicizes textual différance into a critique of imperial epistemic violence.
historicalContext: From Of Grammatology (1976) through A Critique of Postcolonial Reason (1999).

citations.author: Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak
citations.work: Translator's Preface to Of Grammatology / Can the Subaltern Speak?

label: Indicted First-World intellectuals for effacing ideology and subaltern silence
description: In "Can the Subaltern Speak?" (1988), Spivak famously critiqued Foucault and Deleuze's conversation on intellectuals and power, arguing that by collapsing representation (Vertretung/Darstellung), Western post-structuralists smuggle back a transparent sovereign subject.
dialecticalTension: Reveals how even radical European anti-essentialism reproduces epistemic Eurocentrism.
historicalContext: Core intervention in Marxism and the Interpretation of Culture (1988).

label: Synthesized Marxian value and subaltern labor critique with feminist deconstruction
description: Spivak repeatedly returned to Marx's distinction between political proxy (Vertretung) and aesthetic portrait (Darstellung) as well as international divisions of gendered labor to critique global capitalism.
dialecticalTension: Maintains Marxian materialism in productive tension with Derridean deconstruction.
historicalContext: In Other Worlds (1987) and A Critique of Postcolonial Reason (1999).

label: Theorized subaltern foreclosure and epistemic violence under empire
description: Spivak defined epistemic violence as the systemic disqualification of colonized subjects' ways of knowing, demonstrating why the gendered subaltern cannot be heard within dominant colonial or nationalist archives.
dialecticalTension: Shifts ethics from "giving voice" to unlearning First-World intellectual privilege.

label: Co-theorized statelessness, vulnerability, and transnational solidarity
description: Spivak's deconstructive transnationalism shaped Judith Butler's later global turn, culminating in their co-authored philosophical dialogue Who Sings the Nation-State? (2007) on statelessness and performative assembly.
dialecticalTension: Brings postcolonial subaltern analysis into dialogue with performative politics of precariousness.
historicalContext: Spivak and Butler co-authored Who Sings the Nation-State? in 2007.
